ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Oncogenic viruses are infections that can transform normal cells into cancer through genetic and immune mechanisms. Recognising the associated malignancies, transmission routes and preventive strategies guides early detection and management.

sections.p: Certain viruses can initiate or promote cancer by inserting oncogenes, inactivating tumor suppressors, or causing chronic inflammation. Understanding the pathogenesis helps clinicians anticipate malignancies in infected patients.
b: Key mechanisms: insertional mutagenesis, chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, epigenetic changes.

sections.p: Oncogenic viruses include DNA viruses (HPV, EBV, HBV, KSHV) and RNA retroviruses (HTLV‑1). They have tropism for epithelial, lymphoid or endothelial cells and often establish persistent infection.
b: DNA viruses: double‑stranded, often integrate into host genome.
RNA retroviruses: reverse‑transcribe and integrate as provirus.

sections.p: Transmission varies: sexual contact (HPV, HBV), blood (HBV, HTLV‑1), saliva (EBV), vector bite (KSHV), mother‑to‑child (HBV). Persistent infection allows long latency before cancer appears.
b: HPV: skin‑to‑skin, mucosal contact.
HBV: perinatal, sexual, parenteral.
EBV: saliva, organ transplant.
KSHV: sexual, saliva, blood.

sections.p: Each virus is linked to specific malignancies; clinicians must screen at‑risk patients and recognise early signs.
b: HPV – cervical, anal, penile, oropharyngeal, vulvar cancers.
HBV – hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
EBV – nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, gastric carcinoma.
KSHV – Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease.
HTLV‑1 – adult T‑cell leukemia/lymphoma.

sections.p: Diagnosis combines clinical suspicion, serology, molecular testing and histopathology. When resources are limited, prioritize high‑yield tests.
b: If molecular tests unavailable, use surrogate markers (e.g., elevated AFP for HBV‑related HCC) and refer for biopsy.

t.a: HPV DNA PCR or high‑risk HPV mRNA test
t.b: Does the patient have high‑risk HPV infection? Positive result supports risk of cervical/oropharyngeal cancer.
Is there chronic HBV infection? Positive indicates need for HCC surveillance.

t.a: EBV serology (VCA IgG, EBNA) or EBV‑encoded RNA (EBER) in tissue
t.b: Is EBV involved in the tumor? Positive guides diagnosis of EBV‑associated lymphoma or nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

t.a: KSHV PCR on blood or tissue
t.b: Is KSHV present? Positive supports Kaposi sarcoma or related lymphoproliferative disease.
Is HTLV‑1 infection present? Positive indicates risk for adult T‑cell leukemia/lymphoma.

sections.p: Management targets the virus, the malignancy, and supportive care. Vaccination and screening are primary preventive tools.
b: Vaccines: HPV (9‑valent) prevents cervical/oropharyngeal cancers; HBV vaccine prevents HCC.
Antivirals: Nucleos(t)ide analogues for chronic HBV reduce HCC risk; no approved antivirals for HPV or EBV‑related cancers.
Oncologic therapy: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy per cancer type.
Immune restoration: treat HIV co‑infection, avoid immunosuppressive drugs when possible.

sections.p: Key facts that frequently appear in exams.
b: High‑risk HPV types 16/18 cause >70% of cervical cancers.
HBV integration into hepatocyte DNA drives HCC even without cirrhosis.
EBV latency I (c‑Myc translocation) underlies endemic Burkitt lymphoma.
KSHV encodes viral IL‑6, promoting angiogenesis in Kaposi sarcoma.

whenToSeekHelp: Newly diagnosed HCC in a patient with chronic HBV
Rapidly enlarging cervical lesion with abnormal bleeding
Unexplained lymphadenopathy with systemic B symptoms in an EBV‑endemic area

faq.q: Can antiviral therapy cure virus‑related cancers?
faq.a: Antivirals can reduce viral load and lower cancer risk but do not eradicate established tumors; definitive cancer treatment is still required.

faq.q: Why is HPV vaccination given before sexual debut?
faq.a: Vaccination before exposure ensures immunity before the virus can infect the epithelium, providing maximal protection against future cancer.

faq.q: Is liver damage from HBV due to the virus itself?
faq.a: Most liver injury is immune‑mediated; the virus triggers chronic inflammation that leads to fibrosis and cancer.

exam: List five oncogenic viruses and the primary malignancy each causes.
Explain how chronic HBV infection leads to hepatocellular carcinoma despite low viral cytopathic effect.
Describe the role of HPV vaccination in primary prevention of cervical cancer and its impact on public health.
